builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
summary: OutfitterBench replaces generic short-horizon agent evaluations with a 200-day resource-allocation simulation (46-product catalog, ~1,100 reservations, fixed capital ceiling) that tests whether agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing allocation value. Adoption costs integration effort against its public codebase and the API inference budget to run 200-day episodes per model, and it provides no production-ready policy, only a diagnostic. It can fail to transfer if the reader's workload lacks comparable commitment structure, and results may overfit to this rental-domain simulation rather than predict behavior in the reader's actual environment.
rationale: The reader operates agents through APIs and needs realistic failure signals before production deployment, so running this public benchmark is a cheap, workload-relevant validation step rather than an adoption of a new method.

claims.statement: OutfitterBench replaces generic short-horizon agent evaluations with a 200-day resource-allocation simulation (46-product catalog, ~1,100 reservations, fixed capital ceiling) that tests whether agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing allocation value. Adoption costs integration effort against its public codebase and the API inference budget to run 200-day episodes per model, and it provides no production-ready policy, only a diagnostic. It can fail to transfer if the reader's workload lacks comparable commitment structure, and results may overfit to this rental-domain simulation rather than predict behavior in the reader's actual environment.

Only one of seven frontier LLMs consistently outperforms a simple rule-based baseline over 200 simulated days; several agents fall below it, with failures including inconsistent constraint application and decisions conflicting with prior commitments.
